text: The first line of almost every Dockerfile, FROM ubuntu or FROM python, looks like a formality. It isn't. That line decides every package, shared library, and binary that ships inside your container, whether your app ever touches them or not, and every one of those packages is something a scanner can flag and an attacker can abuse.

Think of base images as three tiers. A full distro like ubuntu or debian gives you a shell, apt, and hundreds of libraries you probably don't need. A slim image like python slim still has that shell, but drops documentation and build tools. A distroless image drops the shell and the package manager entirely, leaving just the runtime and whatever you explicitly copy in.

That last point is the whole case for distroless. There's no bin sh in the image, so docker exec dash it into it for a shell simply fails — there's nothing there to give you a prompt. If an attacker gets code execution, a huge category of post-exploitation techniques has no tool to run at all.

You rarely have to pick one image for the whole build. A multi-stage Dockerfile compiles with a full toolchain, like golang, in one stage, then copies only the finished binary into a distroless final stage. The compiler, and everything else in that build stage, never ships.

So which tier should you actually reach for? If you need to shell in and debug directly, stick with slim or Alpine. If you're shipping a compiled or static binary, distroless is almost always the better call. And if you do need to debug a distroless container in production, kubectl debug with an ephemeral container is the tool, not docker exec.

A smaller base image isn't just a faster pull — it's fewer packages for a scanner to flag and less for an attacker to use. Next, we'll put a real scanner to work and see exactly what it finds before any of this ever ships.
